mcqs.question: Why is a hero image referenced by a CSS `background-image` typically discovered much later than one written as `` in the HTML?
options: The preload scanner reads HTML attributes and can start the fetch immediately, but a CSS background is only known once the stylesheet is downloaded and applied
CSS background images are always assigned the lowest network priority regardless of position
Background images cannot be fetched until the whole document has finished parsing
The browser defers all CSS-referenced resources until after the load event fires
mcqs.explanation: The preload scanner races ahead of the main parser looking for `src` and `href` attributes, so an HTML-declared image starts downloading almost immediately; a background image is invisible to it until the CSSOM exists and style is applied to the element. Priority does play a role once the fetch starts, but the delay here is about discovery time, not queue position.

mcqs.question: You want the hero image of the current page to download as early as possible. Which hint is correct?
options: `<link rel="prefetch" as="image" href="hero.avif">`
`<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://cdn.example.com">`
`<link rel="preload" as="image" href="hero.avif" fetchpriority="high">`
`<link rel="preconnect" href="https://cdn.example.com" crossorigin>`
mcqs.explanation: `preload` downloads a resource for the current navigation at a priority you can raise, which is exactly what an LCP image needs. `prefetch` is for a likely *future* navigation and fetches at the lowest priority, so it may arrive after paint; the connection hints save round trips to the host but never start the image download itself.

mcqs.question: A team adds `loading="lazy"` to every image on the page, including the hero. What is the effect on LCP?
options: LCP improves, because fewer images compete for bandwidth during load
LCP is unchanged, since lazy loading only affects images outside the viewport
LCP becomes unmeasurable, because lazy images are excluded as LCP candidates
LCP gets worse, because the hero's fetch is deferred until layout confirms it is in view
mcqs.explanation: Lazy loading delays the request until the browser has laid out enough of the page to know the image is near the viewport, which pushes the LCP element's download later — a common self-inflicted regression. Lazy images remain valid LCP candidates, so the metric is still reported, just worse.

mcqs.question: Your body text uses `font-display: swap` and the swap causes a visible layout shift. What removes the shift without abandoning the web font?
options: Switch to `font-display: block` so text is invisible until the font arrives
Apply `size-adjust` and `ascent-override` so the fallback occupies the same space as the web font
Preload the font file so it arrives before first paint on every connection
Set `font-display: auto` and let the browser choose the best behaviour
mcqs.explanation: The shift comes from the fallback and web font having different metrics, so overriding the fallback's metrics makes the swap change glyphs without changing the space they occupy. `block` trades the shift for up to three seconds of invisible text, and preloading only makes the swap happen sooner — it cannot guarantee arrival before paint on a slow connection.

mcqs.question: Two pages ship the same 400KB gzipped bundle, but one feels far slower on a mid-tier Android phone than on a laptop. Why is the gap so large?
options: Mobile networks cap the download rate for compressed JavaScript files
Phones cannot cache JavaScript across navigations, so it is re-downloaded each time
Parse, compile, and execute are CPU-bound, and a mid-tier phone processes roughly 1MB of JavaScript per second where a laptop is several times faster
Gzip decompression on mobile is significantly slower than on desktop, adding seconds
mcqs.explanation: You pay for JavaScript three times — download, parse/compile, and execute — and the last two are pure CPU work where a mid-tier phone is several times slower than a development laptop, which is why the problem is invisible in development. Caching and decompression exist on both platforms and do not explain a gap of seconds.

mcqs.question: A team adds twelve `preload` hints for fonts, icons, and analytics, and LCP gets worse. Why?
options: Preload priority is zero-sum, so the preloaded resources compete for bandwidth with the LCP image
Preload hints are processed sequentially, so each one delays the next by a full round trip
The browser ignores all preload hints once more than eight are present on a page
Preloaded resources are excluded from the HTTP cache, forcing a second fetch of each
mcqs.explanation: Preload raises priority relative to everything else, so marking twelve resources as high-priority means the LCP image now shares bandwidth with eleven competitors — marking everything important marks nothing important. The hints are fetched in parallel rather than serially, and preloaded responses do populate the cache normally.
